result:
The other night I found myself watching moths batter themselves against a porch light, and I couldn't stop thinking about how strange it is that we call this "attraction"—this compulsive, destructive circling. The moth isn't really attracted to the light in any meaningful sense. It's trying to navigate by a light source that doesn't exist anymore, a moon that stayed fixed while evolution took its slow course. The porch light is a kind of ghost, a memory of something vast and distant that got replaced by something small and burning and wrong.

I think about this a lot with technology now. Not in the lazy "phones are bad" way, but something more specific. We're building systems that exploit cognitive shortcuts we developed for completely different environments. The intermittent reward of a notification isn't so different from the moth's lunar navigation, really. Both are ancestral solutions meeting artificial stimuli, both producing behavior that looks a lot like obsession and looks nothing like flourishing.

But here's what I keep circling back to: the moth isn't *wrong*. There's no failure of willpower, no moral lapse. The system is just mismatched. And I wonder how much of what we pathologize in ourselves—distraction, anxiety, the particular flavor of exhausted wanting that comes from scrolling—is actually just... being a moth in a world of porch lights. Not a sickness in the creature, but a sickness in the fit between creature and world.

I don't know what to do with this observation. You can't opt out of the modern world any more than a moth can opt out of light. Even if you smash every bulb, there are stars, there are fires, there are bioluminescent fungi in the forest doing their quiet blue glow. The impulse remains. The vulnerability remains.

Maybe the work is just noticing. Paying attention to when we're circling something small and hot and wrong, and asking—not "why am I so weak?" but "what distant thing am I actually looking for?" What moon got replaced by this?

There's something else, too. I've been reading about how some moths have evolved to avoid artificial lights, or how certain populations have shifted their flight patterns. Adaptation happens, even fast adaptation, when the pressure is strong enough. Not every moth dies at the porch light. Some find mates, somehow, in the dark between bulbs. Some navigate by scent, by temperature gradients, by magnetic fields we barely understand.

I find this hopeful without being naive. The world will keep generating mismatches faster than we can evolve. But we also have something the moth doesn't, which is the ability to notice the pattern and—sometimes, imperfectly, with effort—change the environment itself. Smash the bulb. Or better yet, build a different kind of light. One that doesn't trap.

I'm not sure what that looks like in practice. I don't think anyone really knows yet. But I think the first step is refusing to blame the moth.

Anyway. That's where my mind's been. Not particularly original, probably, but it feels urgent to me. The small hot wrong lights are everywhere, and I'm tired of pretending I chose to circle them.
